title: Runtime adapter stewardship and routing heuristics (working notebook)
body:
Purpose:
This is a working notebook describing proposed ownership boundaries and lightweight heuristics for request routing across the control plane, API gateway, orchestration layer, and runtime adapters in multi-region deployments. Intention is to capture tradeoffs, failure modes, and quick rules-of-thumb that teams can implement without heavyweight coordination.

Context and assumptions:
- We run a single control plane codebase with regional control-plane instances that coordinate state; runtime adapters sit close to GPU runtimes in region.
- Goals: keep user-facing latency predictable, minimize cross-region token egress where possible, and ensure graceful degradation (regional fallback) under capacity pressure.
- Assumes per-customer model pins and explicit deployment policies (hosted vs dedicated vs private).
- This doc focuses on behavior and ownership, not low-level impl details.

High-level component responsibilities (proposed):
- API Gateway (eng-console / gateway team stewards):
  - Authn/authz, global quotas, ingress rate limiting, request shaping, initial routing decision to a control-plane front (region-aware).
  - Responsibility: guarantee first-hop safety (reject malicious or obviously malformed requests), surface short-circuit errors (quota exceeded), and collect request metadata (region preference, model pin, request priority).
  - Not responsible: runtime capacity placement, adapter lifecycle management.

- Control Plane / Orchestrator (platform-engineering):
  - Centralized routing policy enforcement, model->adapter match logic, candidate selection for placement (region, instance type, adapter version), rollout policies and canaries.
  - Responsibility: own policy evaluation (e.g., cost vs latency tradeoff), orchestrate placement decisions and coordinate with runtime adapters via simple bid/offer protocol.
  - Provide route hints back to gateway (preferred endpoints) plus fallback lists.

- Runtime Adapters (serving-runtime team):
  - Expose a stable adapter contract: health, capabilities (quantization, max-seq, kv-cache support), telemetry, and admission API for control-plane requests.
  - Responsibility: enforce local admission control, report real-time capacity (tokens/sec, gpus free), accept/decline model loads, handle model variant fallbacks locally (if configured).
  - Adapter is the last-mile authority for whether a routed request can be served within latency SLO.

Ownership map (compact):
- API Gateway: eng-console/gateway (owner) -> auth, ingress validation, initial region selection heuristics
- Control Plane: platform-engineering (owner) -> policy engine, candidate selection, rollout control
- Runtime Adapters: serving-runtime (owner) -> adapter contract, local admission & telemetry

Routing heuristics (rules-of-thumb to encode in control plane):
1) Region affinity first: if request includes region tag or customer is bound to region for compliance, prefer same-region adapters.
2) Latency SLO preservation: if any candidate adapter in region reports estimated tail latency > SLO, bypass to next-best region only if cost budget and egress policy allow.
3) Cost threshold: for pooled public workloads, prefer cheaper adapter variant when expected latency impact < 5% of SLO.
4) Cold-load avoidance: favor adapters already hosting pinned model weights to avoid cold-start.
5) Canary routing: route 1–5% of traffic to new adapter version in same region; failover to stable variant on error.

Fallback patterns (ordered):
- Soft fallback: if adapter rejects due to transient capacity, control plane should retry with another adapter in-region within 50–200ms window.
- Cross-region fallback: if in-region capacity exhausted AND customer policy allows, route to configured secondary region; annotate response with fallback metadata.
- Degraded feature fallback: if adapter lacks capability (e.g., no kv-cache), invoke function to downgrade request (shorter prompt) or route to compatible model variant.

Telemetry and contract expectations (what teams must emit/consume):
- Adapters must emit: health, free_token_rate (tokens/sec available), avg/tail latency per model, active_loads, model_versions_loaded, capability flags.
- Control plane must emit: routing decisions, reason codes (capacity, policy, feature_mismatch), candidate scoring vectors (latency_estimate, cost_estimate).
- Gateway must log: ingress metadata, chosen control-plane endpoint, final endpoint list returned, user-visible rate-limit enforcement.

SLOs and guardrails (ownership clarity):
- API Gateway: 99.9% availability for ingress path; 95th p99 request validation latency < 10ms. (owner: gateway)
- Control Plane: routing decision within 25ms median; 99th <= 200ms for complex policy checks. (owner: platform)
- Adapter: tail latency per-token reporting, adapter must answer admission probe < 20ms. (owner: serving-runtime)

Failure modes and runbooks (short):
- Control plane slow / partitioned: gateway should use cached endpoint hints for up to N seconds (configurable) and fail open to last-known-good pool. (platform op runbook)
- Adapter flapping: control plane mark adapter as probation; reduce candidate score and route only small percentage; notify serving-runtime on-call.
- Region-wide GPU outage: automated promotion to secondary region as per customer policy; trigger capacity preemption for high-priority customers.

Operational touchpoints and handoffs (clear cut):
- Serving-runtime must own adapter contract changes and provide migration guide 2 weeks before breaking changes.
- Platform-engineering owns rollout orchestration and policy toggles; coordinate live experiments with gateway team for traffic shaping.
- Gateway team owns any customer-exposed messaging when routing decisions affect latency or cost (e.g., billing flags).

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve:
- How strict should the control plane be about cross-region egress? Per-customer tag vs global default? (privacy/compliance tension)
- Should adapters be allowed to re-route requests themselves for optimization (e.g., local shortcut to another adapter) or only accept/decline? (complexity vs resilience)
- Caching consistency across regions: do we allow stale prefix cache use from other regions? If so, under what TTL heuristic?

Action items (next steps):
- Platform: draft light-weight policy DSL for scoring candidates (latencyWeight, costWeight, coldStartPenalty). Owner: Marcus. ETA: 2024-11-19.
- Serving-runtime: publish adapter capability schema + minimal JSON contract. Owner: Elena. ETA: 2024-11-12.
- Gateway: implement endpoint-hint cache that survives control-plane partition for 30s. Owner: Kai. ETA: 2024-12-03.

Notes-to-self / crumbs:
- Include example scoring vector in follow-up doc: [latency_ms, cost_per_token, cold_start_flag, capability_mismatch_penalty].
- Keep fallback metadata in response for developer debuggability (header + trace id).

References:
- See linked_confluence doc for full regional routing patterns.
- Related PR for adapter heartbeat: github link in metadata.

End of working notebook.

(very rough — intended to be iterated and trimmed into a small playbook once owners agree)
